title: Why is this chapter important?
text:
Why is this chapter important?
• Modern AI is rarely a simple “one input, one task, one output” system.
• Real-world systems often combine multiple data sources and multiple
reasoning objectives.
• Multimodal learning reflects how humans use multiple senses.
• Multitask learning reflects the need for one model to serve multiple
functions.
• This chapter connects deep learning theory with practical system design.
Key message
A correct understanding of fusion, alignment, and loss balancing helps move
from demos to real deployed systems.

title: Why is multimodal learning inevitable?
text:
Why is multimodal learning inevitable?
• Real-world decisions require combining evidence from multiple sources.
• One modality can compensate for noise or missing information in another
modality.
• Web-scale data is naturally multimodal: images + text + metadata.
Application examples
• Finance: prices + news + reports.
• Medicine: images + lab tests + patient records.
• Security: video + audio + metadata.

text:
Why is multitask learning useful?
• Shared representations can improve learning efficiency and reduce
overfitting for tasks with limited labels.
• Auxiliary tasks can act as regularizers1 for the main task.
• It reduces operational cost compared with maintaining many separate
models.
• However, it carries the risk of negative transfer.

title: Early fusion (1/2)
text:
Early fusion (1/2)
• Combine low-level features early so that the model learns interactions
from the beginning.
• Example 1 (very-early, input-level): RGB + depth as 4 input channels.
Xfused = concat(Xrgb, Xdepth, dim = c)
Meaning
The model learns cross-modality interactions from the first layer; this is
simple but sensitive to scale/noise differences between channels.

score_txt = txt_model(txt)
alpha = 0.6

text:
PyTorch code: CLIP-like contrastive loss
def
clip_loss(z_img , z_txt , tau =0.07):
z_img = F.normalize(z_img , dim =-1)
z_txt = F.normalize(z_txt , dim =-1)
logits = (z_img @ z_txt.T) / tau
# (B,B)
y = torch.arange(logits.size (0) , device=logits.device)
li = F. cross_entropy (logits , y)
lt = F. cross_entropy (logits.T, y)
return
0.5 * (li + lt)

text:
Zero-shot with CLIP (2/2)
with
torch.no_grad ():
img_f = model. get_image_features ( pixel_values =batch[" pixel_values "])
txt_f = model. get_text_features (
input_ids=batch["input_ids"],
attention_mask =batch[" attention_mask "]
)
v = F.normalize(img_f , dim=-1)
t = F.normalize(txt_f , dim=-1)
logits = 100.0 * (v @ t.T)
# (1, num_labels )
probs = logits.softmax(dim=-1)
pred = labels[probs.argmax(dim =-1).item ()]
Explanation
• with torch.no grad(): disables gradient computation, reducing memory usage and speeding up
inference.
• F.normalize(x, dim=-1) normalizes embeddings to L2 norm 1, so v @ t.T becomes cosine similarity.

def
siglip_loss (z_img , z_txt):
z_img = F.normalize(z_img , dim =-1)
# (B,D)
z_txt = F.normalize(z_txt , dim =-1)
# (B,D)
logits = z_img @ z_txt.T
# (B,B)
y = torch.eye(logits.size (0), device=logits.device)
# diag =1 (
positive)
sign = 2.0 * y - 1.0
# +1 on diag , -1 off -diag
loss = F.softplus(-sign * logits)
# -log
sigma(sign*logit)
return
loss.mean ()

title: What are cross-attention and grounding?
text:
What are cross-attention and grounding?
• Cross-attention: a mechanism that allows tokens from one modality,
e.g. text, to attend to tokens from another modality, e.g. image, in order
to retrieve relevant context.
• Grounding: attaching language content to concrete perceptual evidence
such as image regions, audio segments, or video frames, instead of
reasoning only at the global level.
• In VLMs, cross-attention is a key mechanism for token/region-level
grounding.
Quick example
The prompt “the dog on the left” requires the model to point to the correct
image region, not merely return the label “dog”.

title: Summary
text:
Summary
• Multimodal learning: choose the right fusion level and aligned data.
• Multitask learning: share representations but control losses and gradient
conflicts.
• Modern AI systems often combine both.
• Tensor shapes, loss formulas, code blocks, and debugging workflows must
be understood clearly.
Conclusion
System thinking (data–model–loss–metric–deployment) is as important as
architecture.
